title: The donkey speaks (Numbers 22)
hookLine: a prophet for hire is stopped by his own donkey

cards: Yes, the Bible has a talking donkey, and the story is funnier than its reputation. Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, and Moab's king, Balak, is terrified.
He can't beat them in battle, so he sends for a well-known seer named Balaam, a man whose curses were said to stick, and offers him a fortune to curse Israel.
Balaam is the one person in the story who's supposed to see what others can't. Hold onto that. Because on the road to Moab, the only one who sees anything is his donkey.

teach.h: THE ANGEL ONLY THE DONKEY SEES.
teach.b: First, the road. An angel of the Lord stands in the road with a drawn sword. Balaam doesn't see it.
The donkey does, and swerves into a field. He beats her back onto the road. Then a narrow path between vineyard walls; the angel again; the donkey presses against the wall and crushes Balaam's foot.
He beats her again. Then a spot so narrow there's no way around, and the donkey simply lies down under him. Furious, he beats her with his staff.

teach.h: WHAT HAVE I DONE TO YOU?
teach.b: God opens the donkey's mouth, and she asks: what have I done to you, that you've struck me these three times? Balaam, without blinking, argues with her: you've made a fool of me; if I had a sword I'd kill you.
And she says, roughly: am I not your donkey, the one you've ridden all your life? Have I ever done this to you before? He has to admit it.
Only then does God open Balaam's eyes, and he sees the angel and falls on his face. The well-known seer couldn't see what was in front of his own animal. Fourth, how it ends.

teach.h: A CURSE THAT COMES OUT A BLESSING.
teach.b: Balaam goes on to Moab, and every time he opens his mouth to curse Israel, a blessing comes out, including a line about a star rising out of Jacob, which Christian readers link to the star the Magi followed.
The man hired to curse can't stop blessing. Saint Benedict, writing his rule for monks, told the abbot to hear even the youngest, because God often shows what is better to them.

how: The Rule of Saint Benedict tells the abbot to call the whole community together for important matters, because the Lord often reveals what is better to the younger, and Benedictine communities still hold such councils.

o: the king of Moab who feared Israel's army
a prophet of Israel who led the people out
a seer hired to curse Israel, who blessed it instead

games.q: who did what on the road — tap the pairs.
p: king of Moab, afraid of Israel

s: Balaam saw the angel first and stopped the donkey
the donkey saw the angel three times. Balaam saw nothing until God opened his eyes.
Balaam argued with the donkey when she spoke
he told her if he had a sword he'd kill her.
Balaam ended up cursing Israel as Balak paid him to
every time he opened his mouth to curse, a blessing came out.

games.q: you're Balaam's donkey. there's an angel with a drawn sword in the road. your rider can't see it and keeps beating you. the path is too narrow to turn. what do you do?
o: walk straight ahead into the sword.
lie down right where you are.
games.why: she lies down under him. he beats her again, and then God opens her mouth: what have I done to you?

practice: Think of a voice you've brushed off lately: your kid, the quiet coworker, someone younger or less important than you, or even your own body swerving off the road, the headache, the tiredness. What has it been saying?
Don't argue the way Balaam did; just hear it out. If you pray, ask God to open your eyes; if not, give that voice two full minutes.

wordCard.voice: Balaam, a seer for hire who couldn't see the angel in the road, though his own donkey could, and said so. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a she-donkey. in the story, Balaam's donkey is female.

carryVoice: Your line: even the donkey knew. Sometimes the warning comes from the least likely place. That's day three hundred eighty-six.
